chapter_note: This chapter is overwhelmingly hagiographic/biographical narrative about Mani’s travels and conflicts with political authorities. It contains no recoverable systematic cosmological-correspondential substrate (no cosmos→cosmos mapping sequences). Two paragraphs incorporate a Johannine “light/darkness” saying (Jn 3), best treated as Christian overlay. The ending pivots into communal exhortation/prayer language, i.e., pastoral institutional address.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Biographical scene-setting with honorific titles (“our master… light enlightener”), Ktesiphon/Shapur narrative—typical hagiographic frame rather than systematic teaching.
Continues episodic court narrative (repeated summons, preaching to Shapur). No cosmological system exposition; functions as travel/mission biography.
Further narrative repetition of Shapur’s summons; purely historiographical framing.
Dialogue anecdote introducing named disciple and request for “two Manis”; interpersonal/hagiographic dialogue, not substrate mapping.
Mani’s first-person self-presentation (“single Mani… came to the world”) in a biographical reply; still frame/legendary voice.
Autobiographical complaint about lack of freedom to preach; first-person mission narrative, not impersonal cosmological instruction.

Contains the Johannine motif/wording “the world loves the darkness… hates the light… works are evil” (Jn 3 in apparatus). Even though embedded in narrative, the vector of entry is the Gospel tradition.
Rhetorical question/request to recount events; functions as dialogue bridge within the hagiographic narrative.
Travel report (sea voyage, India, opposition); historical-episodic rather than cosmological-correspondential mapping.
First-person lament about losing freedom to speak; narrative continuation without systematic teaching structure.
Reintroduces the Johannine “world loves darkness… hates light” line; despite political terms (satraps/governors), the identifiable NT phrasing marks this as Gospel overlay material in context.
Continued itinerary (India→Persia), preaching to “powers and authorities”; still missionary narrative rather than substrate exposition.
Fragmentary narrative appeal to the Father’s protection; devotional/biographical rather than structural cosmology.
Rhetorical comparison of a land tolerating rulers yet not accepting Mani’s message; polemical travel narrative.
Dualist formulae (light/darkness, life/death) occur as a description of Mani’s preaching activity (“I… proclaimed”), not as an impersonal, systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential schema.
Opposition by “ruling-power… demons… race of mankind” framed as persecution narrative; no discrete old teaching segment separable from the autobiographical register.
Babylon/Assyrians itinerary; preaching described again in first-person proclamation terms. Not a numbered/systematic substrate unit.
Persecution by judges/rulers plus appeal to the Father’s help; includes direct address (“you yourselves see”) but remains hagiographic narrative rather than institutional rule or core cosmology.
Rhetorical “See now” plus political hierarchy list; still travel polemic, not church discipline or cosmological mapping.
Medes/Parthians mission episode (“played the harp of wisdom”); narrative comparison of lands and rulers, not substrate correspondences.
Explicit dialogue attribution (“Then the apostle speaks…”) is compilation frame language; the content continues autobiographical conquest/mission imagery (“sown seed of life”).
Concludes the “two Manis” argument by rhetorical world-toleration question; still biographical apologetic.
Metaphorical self-description (“walking on tip-toes”) within mission hardship narrative; not systematic teaching.
Direct communal instruction/exhortation (“All of you, pray…”) with explicit institutional anchor (“holy church”); clearly pastoral layer.
Second-person beatitude/exhortation (“blessed are you… make yourselves strong…”)—application voice aimed at community formation.
Disciple’s encomium/blessing of the apostle (“Blessed am I… our father… Father who sent you”), a doxological hagiographic closing within the dialogue frame.
